perspective:
Gloria Bangura’s available information:

- I am an administrative assistant at a large event planning company; Donald is a part-time bartender at company events. We are coworkers and not personally close, interacting mainly during events.

- During several events, I directly observed Donald seeming distracted and lacking enthusiasm while serving drinks. I approached him and said I noticed he seemed off and asked if everything was okay with his job. He told me he wasn’t as into it as he used to be and that it felt repetitive.

- After reflecting on that conversation, I suspected his job dissatisfaction might be connected to deeper personal issues. I suggested he consider talking to a professional. He said he hadn’t considered that and wasn’t sure if it would help.

- After that, I sensed a shift in his behavior toward me and worried he might resent my suggestion or feel I overstepped. I apologized, explaining I only wanted to help and didn’t mean to make assumptions about his life. He said he was taken aback at first, but knew I meant well, and that it was a lot to process.

- I felt relieved that the tension seemed to ease. I told him about an upcoming project, said I thought it could use his creative input, and asked if he’d be interested in collaborating. He thanked me, said he appreciated it, wanted to be more involved, and thought it sounded like a great opportunity.

- After we worked together on the project, I directly observed his significant contributions and renewed enthusiasm. I publicly acknowledged his work in a team meeting, saying his efforts were crucial to the project’s success. He thanked me, said it meant a lot to him, and expressed that he felt glad to contribute and appreciated.
